title: Epilepsy – Symptoms & Causes
red_flags: Seizure lasting more than 5 minutes (status epilepticus) – call emergency services
Failure to regain consciousness after a seizure
A second seizure occurring shortly after the first
Seizure occurring in water or during other high-risk activities
Seizure in a pregnant woman or someone with diabetes
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الأعصاب
content: Epilepsy is a chronic neurological disorder characterised by recurrent, unprovoked seizures resulting from abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Seizures can manifest in many ways depending on which part of the brain is affected: focal (partial) seizures affect one area and may cause twitching, sensory changes, or altered awareness; generalised seizures involve the whole brain and include tonic-clonic (grand mal) seizures with rhythmic jerking movements and loss of consciousness, absence seizures (brief staring spells), myoclonic jerks, atonic ('drop') attacks, and tonic seizures. Diagnosis is primarily clinical, supported by electroencephalography (EEG) and neuroimaging (MRI). Common causes include genetic factors, brain injury, stroke, brain tumours, and infections. Antiseizure medications (ASMs) such as levetiracetam, valproate, lamotrigine, and carbamazepine control seizures in about 70% of patients. Drug-resistant epilepsy may be managed with ketogenic diet, vagus nerve stimulation, or epilepsy surgery. Status epilepticus (a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes or repeated seizures without recovery) is a life-threatening emergency requiring immediate emergency services. Patients with epilepsy should be counselled on safety (driving restrictions, swimming precautions, medication adherence) and should wear a medical alert bracelet.

title: Tinnitus – Symptoms, Causes & Treatment
red_flags: Pulsatile tinnitus (heartbeat sound in ear) – may indicate vascular abnormality
Sudden one-sided hearing loss with tinnitus
Tinnitus with neurological symptoms (dizziness, facial weakness, speech difficulty)
Rapidly progressive tinnitus with hearing loss in both ears
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الأنف والأذن والحنجرة
content: Tinnitus is the perception of sound in the ears or head when no external sound source is present. It is commonly described as ringing, buzzing, hissing, whistling, whooshing, or clicking. Tinnitus is very common and affects up to 15% of the general population. In most cases it is a symptom rather than a disease itself, arising from disorders of the auditory system including noise-induced hearing loss, age-related hearing loss (presbycusis), earwax build-up, ear infections, Ménière's disease, otosclerosis, and certain medications (ototoxic drugs such as high-dose aspirin, loop diuretics, aminoglycoside antibiotics, and platinum-based chemotherapy). Pulsatile tinnitus synchronised with the heartbeat warrants urgent investigation to exclude vascular causes such as arteriovenous malformation, carotid artery stenosis, or glomus tumour. Sudden-onset unilateral tinnitus with hearing loss may indicate sudden sensorineural hearing loss, a medical emergency requiring urgent ENT assessment and oral corticosteroids. Although there is no cure for most forms of chronic tinnitus, management strategies include sound therapy, hearing aids (if hearing loss is present), cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), and tinnitus retraining therapy (TRT) to help the brain habituate to the perceived sound and reduce its impact on quality of life.

title: Pancreatitis – Symptoms, Causes & Treatment
red_flags: Severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back
Fever with rapid heart rate and abdominal pain
Yellowing of the skin and eyes (jaundice) with severe abdominal pain
Vomiting that cannot be controlled with abdominal pain
recommended_specialty_ar: الجهاز الهضمي والجراحة العامة أو طوارئ المستشفى
content: Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas that can occur as a sudden acute episode or as a long-term chronic condition. Acute pancreatitis most commonly presents with sudden severe pain in the upper abdomen that may radiate to the back, often described as a persistent dull ache or severe boring pain that is worse when lying flat and slightly relieved by leaning forwards. Associated symptoms include nausea, vomiting, fever, rapid heartbeat, and in severe cases jaundice, diarrhoea, and indigestion. The two most common causes of acute pancreatitis are gallstones (which block the pancreatic duct) and excessive alcohol consumption. Other causes include hypertriglyceridaemia, hypercalcaemia, certain medications (azathioprine, thiazide diuretics), and trauma. Severity is assessed using scoring systems (Ranson criteria, APACHE II, BISAP); severe acute pancreatitis with organ failure carries a mortality of up to 30%. Management includes IV fluid resuscitation, analgesia, nutritional support (early enteral feeding is preferred), and treatment of the underlying cause. Chronic pancreatitis results in progressive destruction of pancreatic tissue, causing chronic pain, exocrine insufficiency (malabsorption, steatorrhoea), and endocrine insufficiency (diabetes mellitus). All cases of suspected acute pancreatitis require hospital admission.

title: Hepatitis B – WHO Fact Sheet
red_flags: Jaundice (yellow skin and eyes) with dark urine
Severe fatigue with right upper quadrant abdominal pain
Swelling of the abdomen (ascites) with jaundice
Confusion or altered consciousness in a patient with liver disease (hepatic encephalopathy)
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الجهاز الهضمي والكبد
content: Hepatitis B is a potentially life-threatening liver infection caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV). It is a major global health problem and can cause chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, and hepatocellular carcinoma (liver cancer). HBV is transmitted through contact with the blood or other body fluids (semen, vaginal secretions) of an infected person, through perinatal transmission from mother to child, through sexual contact, and through sharing of contaminated needles. The incubation period is 30 to 180 days. Acute hepatitis B presents with jaundice (yellowing of the skin and whites of the eyes), dark urine, fatigue, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain. Most adults (over 95%) clear the infection spontaneously; however, 5–10% develop chronic infection. The risk of chronicity is highest in those infected in infancy (up to 90%). Chronic hepatitis B may be asymptomatic for decades before progressing to cirrhosis or liver cancer. Diagnosis is confirmed by serological markers (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs) and HBV DNA. Antiviral therapy (tenofovir or entecavir) suppresses viral replication and reduces complications but rarely achieves a cure. The hepatitis B vaccine is safe and highly effective (90–95% protection), and vaccination is the cornerstone of prevention. WHO recommends universal infant vaccination and vaccination of high-risk groups. Signs of acute liver failure (encephalopathy, coagulopathy, jaundice) require immediate emergency hospital admission.

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease – Symptoms & Causes
red_flags: Severe abdominal pain with rigidity or rebound tenderness (suspected perforation)
Significant rectal bleeding with haemodynamic compromise
High fever with severe diarrhoea and abdominal distension (toxic megacolon)
Rapid unintentional weight loss with bloody stool
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الجهاز الهضمي
content: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a term that encompasses two main chronic, relapsing inflammatory conditions of the gastrointestinal tract: Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis. Crohn's disease can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus, with transmural (full-thickness) inflammation and skip lesions being characteristic features. Ulcerative colitis is limited to the colon and rectum, with continuous mucosal inflammation. Common symptoms of IBD include persistent diarrhoea (often with blood or mucus), abdominal pain and cramping, rectal bleeding, unintentional weight loss, fatigue, and urgency to defecate. Extra-intestinal manifestations are common and include arthritis, uveitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis, skin lesions (erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum), and anaemia. Diagnosis is made through a combination of clinical assessment, laboratory tests (full blood count, CRP, faecal calprotectin), endoscopy with biopsy, and imaging (MRI enterography, CT). Treatment aims to induce and maintain remission using aminosalicylates (for ulcerative colitis), corticosteroids (for acute flares), immunomodulators (azathioprine, 6-mercaptopurine, methotrexate), and biological therapies (anti-TNF agents such as infliximab and adalimumab, anti-integrin agents such as vedolizumab). Surgery may be required for complications such as perforation, fistula, stricture, or refractory disease. Regular colonoscopic surveillance is recommended due to the increased risk of colorectal cancer in long-standing colitis.

title: Fibromyalgia – Symptoms, Causes & Treatment
red_flags: Widespread pain with new neurological deficits (requires urgent investigation)
Severe unexplained weight loss with diffuse pain
High fever with diffuse muscle and joint pain (exclude septic arthritis or systemic infection)
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الروماتيزم والعظام والعلاج الطبيعي
content: Fibromyalgia is a long-term condition characterised by widespread musculoskeletal pain, fatigue, sleep disturbance, and often cognitive difficulties ('fibro fog'). It is one of the most common musculoskeletal conditions, affecting approximately 2–4% of the population, with a significantly higher prevalence in women. The pain of fibromyalgia is typically described as a constant dull ache felt throughout the body, often worse in the morning and exacerbated by cold, stress, or physical activity. Associated symptoms include headaches (including migraine), irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), urinary frequency, restless legs syndrome, anxiety, and depression. The exact cause is not fully understood, but central sensitisation – an amplified pain response due to altered pain processing in the central nervous system – is the leading hypothesis. Diagnosis is clinical (based on the revised 2016 ACR diagnostic criteria) after excluding other conditions with blood tests and imaging. There is no cure, but a multimodal approach combining pharmacological therapy (low-dose amitriptyline, duloxetine, pregabalin), structured graded exercise therapy, cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT), sleep hygiene measures, and patient education has the best evidence. Opioids are not recommended. Referral to rheumatology is appropriate when the diagnosis is uncertain or the condition is refractory to initial management.

title: Osteoporosis – Symptoms & Causes
red_flags: Sudden back pain after minimal trauma (suspected vertebral fracture)
Loss of height or spinal deformity (kyphosis) suggesting vertebral collapse
Hip pain with inability to weight-bear after a fall in an older patient
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض العظام والروماتيزم
content: Osteoporosis is a systemic skeletal disease characterised by low bone mass and deterioration of bone microarchitecture, resulting in increased bone fragility and susceptibility to fracture. It is often called a 'silent disease' because bone loss occurs without symptoms until a fracture occurs. The most common osteoporotic fracture sites are the vertebral column (spine), hip (proximal femur), and wrist (Colles' fracture). Vertebral compression fractures cause acute or chronic back pain, loss of height, and progressive kyphosis ('dowager's hump'). Hip fractures in the elderly are associated with significant morbidity and mortality. Risk factors include advancing age, female sex (especially post-menopause due to oestrogen deficiency), low body weight, smoking, excessive alcohol consumption, prolonged corticosteroid use, calcium and vitamin D deficiency, immobility, and a family history of osteoporosis or fracture. Diagnosis is made by dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA) measuring bone mineral density (BMD); a T-score of -2.5 or below defines osteoporosis. The FRAX tool estimates 10-year fracture probability. Prevention and treatment include adequate calcium and vitamin D supplementation, weight-bearing exercise, fall prevention, and pharmacological therapy: bisphosphonates (alendronate, risedronate) are first-line; alternatives include denosumab, raloxifene, teriparatide, and romosozumab.

title: Musculoskeletal Conditions – WHO Fact Sheet
red_flags: Sudden joint swelling with fever suggesting septic arthritis
Bone pain in an older adult with unexplained weight loss (exclude malignancy)
Spinal pain with neurological deficits in the limbs (cauda equina or cord compression)
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الروماتيزم والعظام والعلاج الطبيعي
content: Musculoskeletal conditions comprise more than 150 different diseases and syndromes that affect the locomotor system including joints, bones, muscles, spine, and connective tissues. They are the leading cause of disability worldwide, with low back pain being the single leading cause of disability globally. Other major musculoskeletal conditions include osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, osteoporosis, and fibromyalgia. These conditions are characterised by pain (often persistent), limited mobility, reduced dexterity and functional ability, early retirement from work, and reduced ability to participate in social roles. WHO's Global Action Plan on Physical Activity and the rehabilitation framework both emphasise the importance of early intervention. Risk factors include ageing, obesity, physical inactivity, occupational hazards (heavy lifting, repetitive motions), smoking, and metabolic factors. Management strategies include physical and occupational therapy, exercise programmes (strength training, aerobic exercise), weight reduction, assistive devices, pain management (analgesics, NSAIDs), disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) for inflammatory arthritides, and surgery where appropriate. Septic arthritis (joint infection) is a medical emergency requiring immediate hospitalisation, joint aspiration, and intravenous antibiotics to prevent permanent joint destruction.

title: Lupus – Symptoms, Causes & Treatment
red_flags: Severe chest pain or breathlessness (lupus pleuritis or pericarditis)
Seizures or confusion in a patient with known lupus (neuropsychiatric lupus)
Significant reduction in urine output with leg swelling (lupus nephritis)
Very low blood counts causing bleeding or severe infection
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الروماتيزم والمناعة
content: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE or lupus) is a chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks healthy tissue throughout the body, causing inflammation and damage to multiple organ systems. It predominantly affects women of childbearing age, with a female-to-male ratio of approximately 9:1, and is more common and often more severe in people of African, Caribbean, and Asian descent. Lupus is characterised by periods of flare (worsening symptoms) and remission. Common features include a butterfly-shaped (malar) rash across the cheeks and nose, photosensitivity (skin rash worsening with sun exposure), joint pain and swelling (arthralgia and arthritis), extreme fatigue, mouth ulcers, hair loss, serositis (pleuritis and pericarditis), kidney disease (lupus nephritis), and haematological abnormalities (anaemia, leucopenia, thrombocytopenia). Diagnosis requires clinical assessment and laboratory tests including ANA, anti-dsDNA antibodies, complement levels (C3, C4), and urinalysis. Classification uses the 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria. Treatment is tailored to disease severity: hydroxychloroquine is the cornerstone of therapy for all patients; corticosteroids are used for acute flares; immunosuppressants (mycophenolate mofetil, azathioprine, cyclophosphamide, belimumab) are added for organ-threatening disease. Lupus in pregnancy requires specialist management due to increased risk of flares, pre-eclampsia, and neonatal lupus.

title: Dengue and Severe Dengue – WHO Fact Sheet
red_flags: Severe abdominal pain or tenderness during dengue fever
Persistent vomiting with dengue
Bleeding from the gums, nose, or in the stool with fever
Rapid breathing or difficulty breathing with dengue
Fatigue, restlessness, or irritability during the critical phase (warning signs of severe dengue)
recommended_specialty_ar: الأمراض المعدية والباطنة العامة أو طوارئ المستشفى
content: Dengue is a viral mosquito-borne illness caused by any one of four dengue virus serotypes (DENV-1 to DENV-4), transmitted primarily by the Aedes aegypti mosquito. It is the most rapidly spreading mosquito-borne viral disease globally, with an estimated 390 million infections per year. Most infections (up to 75%) are asymptomatic. Symptomatic dengue presents with a sudden high fever (above 38.5°C), severe headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle and joint pain (hence the name 'breakbone fever'), nausea, vomiting, and a characteristic skin rash. The illness typically passes through three phases: febrile (days 1–3), critical (days 4–6), and recovery (days 7–10). The critical phase is when plasma leakage, haemorrhage, and organ dysfunction can occur. Warning signs of severe dengue that mandate immediate hospitalisation include severe abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, rapid breathing, bleeding gums, fatigue and restlessness, blood in vomit, and clinical deterioration as the fever subsides. Severe dengue can lead to dengue haemorrhagic fever, dengue shock syndrome, and death if not managed promptly. There is no specific antiviral treatment; management is supportive with careful fluid management and monitoring. Prevention relies on mosquito control and the dengue vaccine (Dengvaxia), which is recommended only for seropositive individuals.

title: Psoriasis – Symptoms, Causes & Treatment
red_flags: Erythrodermic psoriasis (generalised redness covering most of the body) – medical emergency
Pustular psoriasis with fever and systemic illness
Swollen, painful joints with psoriasis (psoriatic arthritis requiring urgent rheumatology assessment)
Psoriasis with severe chest pain (exclude psoriatic cardiovascular disease)
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الجلد (الأمراض الجلدية)
content: Psoriasis is a chronic, immune-mediated inflammatory skin condition characterised by well-defined, red or pink plaques covered with silvery-white scales. It affects approximately 2–3% of the global population and can develop at any age, with two peak incidences: between 15–35 years and 50–60 years. The most common form is plaque psoriasis (psoriasis vulgaris), typically affecting the scalp, elbows, knees, and lower back. Other forms include guttate psoriasis (small raindrop-shaped lesions, often triggered by streptococcal throat infection), inverse (flexural) psoriasis, pustular psoriasis (white sterile pustules), and erythrodermic psoriasis (a severe form with generalised skin redness and exfoliation that is a dermatological emergency). Psoriasis is associated with significant comorbidities including psoriatic arthritis (affecting 20–30% of patients), cardiovascular disease, metabolic syndrome, depression, and anxiety. Triggers include skin injury (Koebner phenomenon), infection, stress, smoking, alcohol, and certain medications (lithium, beta-blockers, antimalarials). Treatment is stepwise: topical therapies (corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues, coal tar, retinoids) for mild disease; phototherapy (narrowband UVB) for moderate disease; systemic agents (methotrexate, ciclosporin, acitretin) and biological therapies (TNF-inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors, IL-23 inhibitors) for moderate-to-severe disease. Biologics have revolutionised the treatment of moderate-to-severe psoriasis, achieving skin clearance in a majority of patients.

title: Heart Failure – Symptoms, Causes & Urgent Warning Signs
red_flags: Sudden severe shortness of breath at rest or waking up gasping for air (paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea)
Pink, frothy sputum with acute breathlessness (acute pulmonary edema)
Rapidly worsening ankle, leg, or abdominal swelling with sudden weight gain
Syncope, chest pain, or severe dizziness alongside known cardiac dysfunction
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض القلب والأوعية الدموية / الباطنة العامة
content: Heart failure means the heart is unable to pump blood around the body properly, usually because it has become too stiff or weak. Common symptoms include breathlessness after activity or at rest, feeling tired most of the time, swollen ankles and legs (peripheral edema), and needing extra pillows to sleep flat (orthopnea). Causes include coronary heart disease, high blood pressure, cardiomyopathy, heart valve disease, and arrhythmias. Patients with acute decompensation or pink frothy sputum require immediate emergency care.

title: Asthma – Acute Exacerbation Red Flags & Respiratory Management
red_flags: Reliever inhaler (salbutamol) not relieving wheezing or breathlessness
Inability to speak full sentences, eat, or sleep due to breathing difficulty
Blue lips or fingernails (cyanosis) or silent chest on auscultation
Rapid breathing (tachypnea) with chest wall retractions
recommended_specialty_ar: الأمراض الصدرية والجهاز التنفسي / الحساسية والمناعة
content: Asthma is a common long-term inflammatory condition of the airways causing wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, and coughing, often worse at night or early morning. Triggers include allergens, cold air, exercise, smoke, and viral respiratory infections. Treatment uses inhaled corticosteroids (preventer) and short-acting beta-agonists (reliever). Severe asthma attacks where the reliever inhaler fails or speech is limited are life-threatening emergencies requiring immediate hospital oxygen and nebulized bronchodilators.

title: Pneumonia – Lower Respiratory Infection Triage & Sepsis Red Flags
red_flags: Coughing up blood or rust-colored sputum with high fever and rigors
Rapid shallow breathing, chest pain on inspiration, or low oxygen saturation
New confusion, drowsiness, or difficulty waking in older adults
Bluish skin or lips and cold clammy extremities
recommended_specialty_ar: الأمراض الصدرية والجهاز التنفسي / الباطنة العامة
content: Pneumonia is inflammation of the tissue in one or both lungs, usually caused by a bacterial or viral infection. Symptoms include a productive cough with yellow, green, or blood-stained phlegm, difficulty breathing, rapid heartbeat, high temperature, sweating, shivering, loss of appetite, and pleuritic chest pain. Mild cases are treated with rest, fluids, and oral antibiotics if bacterial, while severe pneumonia requires urgent hospital admission.

title: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) – Unilateral Leg Swelling & Embolism Risk
red_flags: Sudden shortness of breath, sharp pleuritic chest pain, or coughing up blood (pulmonary embolism)
Unilateral calf or thigh swelling, warmth, redness, and cramping pain
Dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting accompanying leg swelling
recommended_specialty_ar: جراحة الأوعية الدموية / أمراض القلب والباطنة
content: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) occurs when a blood clot forms in one or more deep veins, usually in the legs. Symptoms include unilateral leg swelling, cramping pain starting in the calf, red or discolored skin, and a feeling of warmth in the affected leg. Risk factors include prolonged immobility, recent surgery, pregnancy, cancer, and clotting disorders. DVT requires urgent evaluation because a clot can travel to the lungs and cause a life-threatening pulmonary embolism.

title: Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) – WHO Fact Sheet
red_flags: Acute worsening of dyspnea with purulent sputum and confusion (hypercapnic respiratory failure)
Central cyanosis, drowsiness, or inability to clear airway secretions
New peripheral edema suggesting cor pulmonale
recommended_specialty_ar: الأمراض الصدرية والجهاز التنفسي
content: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is a progressive lung disease causing persistent airflow limitation and breathing difficulties, primarily caused by tobacco smoking and indoor or outdoor air pollution. Symptoms include chronic productive cough (smoker's cough), wheezing, progressive exertional breathlessness, and frequent chest infections. Management includes smoking cessation, inhaled bronchodilators, pulmonary rehabilitation, and prompt treatment of acute exacerbations.

title: Pericarditis and Myocarditis – Positional Chest Pain Triage
red_flags: Sharp central chest pain accompanied by hypotension, muffled heart sounds, or severe breathlessness (cardiac tamponade)
Chest pain with syncope, sustained palpitations, or signs of acute heart failure
Chest pain indistinguishable from acute myocardial infarction
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض القلب والأوعية الدموية
content: Pericarditis is inflammation of the protective sac surrounding the heart, often following a viral infection. It typically causes a sharp, stabbing central or left-sided chest pain that worsens when lying flat or breathing deeply and improves when sitting up and leaning forward. Because pericarditis symptoms mimic a heart attack, any acute chest pain requires urgent medical evaluation with ECG and cardiac biomarkers.

title: Migraine – Aura, Photophobia & Stroke Differentiation
red_flags: Sudden explosive thunderclap headache reaching peak intensity within seconds
Headache with fever, neck stiffness, non-blanching rash, or confusion
New-onset severe headache with persistent unilateral weakness, slurred speech, or vision loss
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض المخ والأعصاب
content: A migraine is usually a moderate or severe headache felt as a throbbing pain on one side of the head, often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and increased sensitivity to light (photophobia) and sound (phonophobia). Some people experience temporary visual or sensory aura warning signs before the headache starts. Management involves acute analgesics, triptans, antiemetics, and preventive therapy for frequent attacks.

title: Bell's Palsy – Acute Facial Weakness vs Stroke Triage
red_flags: Facial droop accompanied by arm or leg weakness, slurred speech, or severe vertigo (suspected stroke)
Facial paralysis with severe ear pain and vesicles in the ear canal (Ramsay Hunt syndrome)
Inability to close the eye completely risking corneal ulceration
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض المخ والأعصاب / الأنف والأذن والحنجرة
content: Bell's palsy causes temporary weakness or paralysis of the muscles on one side of the face, including the forehead, resulting in drooping of the mouth and difficulty closing the eye on the affected side. Unlike stroke, which usually spares the upper forehead, Bell's palsy affects the entire half of the face. Urgent medical assessment within 72 hours is essential to exclude stroke and start oral corticosteroids.

title: Conjunctivitis and Red Eye – Ophthalmic Triage & Corneal Red Flags
red_flags: Moderate-to-severe eye pain, marked photophobia, or reduced visual acuity
Red eye in a contact lens wearer (suspected microbial keratitis)
Cloudy cornea, fixed dilated pupil, or halos around lights (acute glaucoma)
recommended_specialty_ar: طب وجراحة العيون
content: Conjunctivitis (red or pink eye) is inflammation of the conjunctiva caused by viral or bacterial infection or allergies. Typical symptoms include bloodshot eyes, burning or gritty sensation, watering, and sticky pus coating the eyelashes without severe pain or vision loss. Any red eye accompanied by severe pain, extreme light sensitivity, or blurred vision requires urgent ophthalmology evaluation.

title: Tonsillitis and Quinsy – Severe Sore Throat & Airway Red Flags
red_flags: Difficulty breathing, stridor, drooling, or inability to swallow saliva (epiglottitis / airway compromise)
Severe unilateral throat pain with muffled 'hot potato' voice, trismus, and uvular deviation (peritonsillar abscess / quinsy)
High fever with neck stiffness or severe dehydration
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الأنف والأذن والحنجرة
content: Tonsillitis is inflammation of the tonsils causing sore throat, pain on swallowing, high temperature, swollen neck lymph nodes, and white pus-filled spots on the tonsils. Most cases are viral and resolve within a week with rest, hydration, and analgesia. Severe unilateral swelling preventing mouth opening or swallowing requires urgent ENT drainage for suspected peritonsillar abscess.

title: Peripheral Neuropathy – Glove-and-Stocking Numbness & Tingling
red_flags: Rapidly ascending numbness and leg weakness over hours to days (Guillain-Barré syndrome)
Foot numbness accompanied by non-healing foot ulcers, redness, or fever (diabetic foot infection)
Numbness with loss of bowel or bladder control
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض المخ والأعصاب / الغدد الصماء والسكري
content: Peripheral neuropathy results from damage to nerves outside the brain and spinal cord, most commonly due to diabetes mellitus, vitamin B12 deficiency, or autoimmune disease. Symptoms include gradual onset of numbness, prickling, or tingling in the feet or hands spreading upward, sharp jabbing or burning pain, and extreme sensitivity to touch. Evaluation includes blood glucose, HbA1c, vitamin B12 levels, and nerve conduction studies.

title: Trigeminal Neuralgia – Electric-Shock Facial Pain Triage
red_flags: Facial pain accompanied by permanent facial numbness, hearing loss, or double vision
Temporal headache with jaw claudication and scalp tenderness in patients over 50 (giant cell arteritis)
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض المخ والأعصاب
content: Trigeminal neuralgia causes sudden, severe, electric-shock-like episodes of pain on one side of the face along the distribution of the trigeminal nerve. Attacks last from a few seconds to two minutes and are triggered by light touch, chewing, speaking, brushing teeth, or cold wind. Diagnosis is clinical with brain MRI to rule out vascular compression or demyelination, and first-line treatment is carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine.

title: Appendicitis – Right Iliac Fossa Pain & Peritonitis Red Flags
red_flags: Pain migrating from the periumbilical area to the lower right abdomen with guarding and rebound tenderness
Sudden temporary relief of severe pain followed by rigid abdomen and high fever (perforated appendix)
Persistent vomiting, tachycardia, and inability to pass gas
recommended_specialty_ar: الجراحة العامة / طوارئ الجهاز الهضمي
content: Appendicitis is painful swelling of the appendix that typically begins with a dull ache around the belly button before shifting to the lower right-hand side of the abdomen and becoming sharp and constant. Movement, coughing, or pressing on the area worsens the pain, often accompanied by nausea, loss of appetite, and low-grade fever. Suspected appendicitis is a surgical emergency requiring urgent hospital assessment.

title: Gallstones and Acute Cholecystitis – Biliary Colic & Jaundice Triage
red_flags: Right upper quadrant pain with high fever, rigors, and jaundice (Charcot's triad / acute cholangitis)
Severe persistent epigastric pain radiating to the back with vomiting (gallstone pancreatitis)
Yellowing of skin and eyes with dark urine and pale stools
recommended_specialty_ar: الجراحة العامة / الجهاز الهضمي والكبد
content: Gallstones can block bile ducts and trigger biliary colic—sudden, intense gripping pain in the upper right abdomen or center of the stomach lasting 1 to 5 hours, often after fatty meals and radiating to the right shoulder blade. If the gallbladder becomes infected (acute cholecystitis), pain becomes constant with fever and tenderness. Ultrasound and liver function tests guide surgical management.

title: Irritable Bowel Syndrome (IBS) – Functional Bowel Symptoms & Red Flags
red_flags: Rectal bleeding or blood mixed with stool
Unexplained weight loss or persistent diarrhea waking the patient from sleep
Iron-deficiency anemia or family history of bowel or ovarian cancer
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الجهاز الهضمي والباطنة العامة
content: Irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) is a common functional disorder affecting the digestive system, causing recurrent stomach cramps, bloating, excess gas, diarrhea, and constipation that fluctuate over time and are often relieved after passing stool. Management includes dietary adjustments (such as low-FODMAP guidance), soluble fiber, antispasmodics, and stress reduction once inflammatory or malignant red flags are excluded.

title: Piles (Hemorrhoids) and Anal Fissure – Bright Red Rectal Bleeding Triage
red_flags: Dark red or black tarry stools (melena) or large-volume rectal hemorrhage with dizziness
Rectal bleeding accompanied by unexplained weight loss, persistent change in bowel habit, or abdominal mass
Severe throbbing perianal swelling with high fever (perianal abscess)
recommended_specialty_ar: الجراحة العامة وجراحة القولون والشرج
content: Hemorrhoids (piles) are swollen blood vessels inside or around the bottom (rectum and anus). Symptoms include bright red blood on toilet paper after passing stool, an itchy or sore anus, and lumps hanging down around the anus. Anal fissures cause sharp tearing pain during bowel movements. High-fiber diet, hydration, and topical treatments help mild cases, while persistent bleeding requires medical examination.

title: Peptic Ulcer Disease – Epigastric Pain & Perforation/Bleeding Alarm Signs
red_flags: Sudden, severe, agonizing upper abdominal pain with board-like abdominal rigidity (perforated ulcer)
Vomiting blood or dark coffee-ground material, or passing black tarry stools
Unexplained weight loss, early satiety, or persistent vomiting
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الجهاز الهضمي والكبد والمناظير
content: Peptic ulcers are open sores on the inside lining of the stomach (gastric ulcers) and upper small intestine (duodenal ulcers), most commonly caused by Helicobacter pylori infection or long-term NSAID pain reliever use. The classic symptom is burning stomach pain between meals or at night that temporarily improves with food or antacids. Upper endoscopy and H. pylori testing confirm the diagnosis.

title: Cholera and Acute Watery Diarrheal Disease – Dehydration Triage
red_flags: Profuse watery 'rice-water' diarrhea with sunken eyes, dry mucous membranes, lethargy, and low urine output (severe dehydration)
Inability to keep oral fluids down due to intractable vomiting
Cold clammy skin, rapid weak pulse, or altered consciousness (hypovolemic shock)
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الجهاز الهضمي / الحميات والأمراض المعدية
content: Acute severe watery diarrhea caused by enteric pathogens such as Vibrio cholerae can lead to life-threatening dehydration and electrolyte imbalance within hours if untreated. Early administration of oral rehydration salts (ORS) treats most mild-to-moderate cases, while patients with severe dehydration or persistent vomiting require urgent intravenous fluid resuscitation.

title: Osteoarthritis – Degenerative Joint Pain, Stiffness & Mobility Triage
red_flags: Single hot, red, acutely swollen joint with fever and inability to bear weight (septic arthritis)
Sudden joint locking or acute trauma with deformity
Systemic symptoms such as unexplained weight loss or night sweats
recommended_specialty_ar: جراحة العظام والمفاصل / الروماتيزم والتأهيل
content: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint condition causing joints to become painful and stiff, most commonly affecting the knees, hips, and small joints of the hands. Pain typically worsens with weight-bearing movement and improves with rest, with brief morning stiffness lasting under 30 minutes and grating or crackling sensations (crepitus). Management focuses on targeted exercise, weight management, analgesia, and physiotherapy.

title: Gout – Acute Podagra & Crystal Arthropathy Triage
red_flags: Hot, swollen, erythematous joint accompanied by high fever and chills (must exclude septic arthritis)
Rapidly spreading redness up the limb (cellulitis)
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الروماتيزم والمناعة / الباطنة العامة
content: Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by uric acid crystals accumulating inside a joint. It typically causes sudden, severe throbbing pain, swelling, heat, and shiny red skin—most classically at the base of the big toe (podagra)—often starting overnight and peaking within hours. Acute flares are treated with NSAIDs or colchicine, followed by long-term urate-lowering therapy such as allopurinol.

title: Rheumatoid Arthritis – Symmetrical Inflammatory Polyarthritis Triage
red_flags: Neck pain with hand numbness, tingling, or walking difficulty (atlantoaxial subluxation / cervical myelopathy)
Single acutely hot swollen joint with fever (septic arthritis in immunosuppressed patient)
Sudden red painful eye (scleritis) or acute breathlessness
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الروماتيزم والمناعة
content: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic autoimmune disease causing symmetrical pain, swelling, and stiffness in multiple joints—most commonly the small joints of the hands, wrists, and feet. Morning stiffness typically lasts more than 30 to 60 minutes and improves with gentle movement, often accompanied by fatigue. Early rheumatology referral for disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) prevents permanent joint damage.

title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome – Median Nerve Compression in Hand & Wrist
red_flags: Visible wasting (atrophy) of the thumb base muscles or permanent loss of grip strength
Acute wrist swelling and numbness after trauma (acute compartment or fracture compression)
recommended_specialty_ar: جراحة العظام وجراحة اليد / أمراض المخ والأعصاب
content: Carpal tunnel syndrome is caused by pressure on the median nerve as it passes through the wrist. Symptoms include tingling, numbness, and burning pain in the thumb, index, middle, and ring fingers—frequently waking patients at night—along with hand weakness and dropping objects. Treatment starts with nocturnal wrist splinting and activity modification, progressing to corticosteroid injection or surgical release.

title: Rotator Cuff Injury and Frozen Shoulder – Shoulder Pain Triage
red_flags: Left shoulder pain accompanied by chest tightness, sweating, or shortness of breath (cardiac ischemia)
Complete inability to lift the arm after acute fall or trauma (acute tear or dislocation)
Hot swollen shoulder with fever (septic arthritis)
recommended_specialty_ar: جراحة العظام وإصابات الملاعب / العلاج الطبيعي
content: Rotator cuff tendinitis or tears cause a dull ache deep in the shoulder that worsens when lifting the arm overhead, reaching behind the back, or lying on the affected side at night, often accompanied by arm weakness. Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder) causes progressive stiffness and loss of both active and passive range of motion. Physiotherapy, targeted exercises, and imaging guide treatment.

title: Plantar Fasciitis – Heel Pain Triage & Mechanical Foot Care
red_flags: Heel pain with visible deformity, bruising, and inability to put any weight on the foot after trauma (calcaneal fracture)
Red, hot, swollen foot with fever or numbness in a diabetic patient (Charcot foot or infection)
recommended_specialty_ar: جراحة العظام والقدم والكاحل / العلاج الطبيعي
content: Plantar fasciitis is inflammation of the thick band of tissue running across the bottom of the foot connecting the heel bone to the toes. The hallmark symptom is sharp stabbing pain under the heel or arch that is worst with the first steps out of bed in the morning or after prolonged rest, easing slightly with walking before returning after long standing. Supportive footwear, calf stretching, and rest relieve most cases.

title: Shingles (Herpes Zoster) – Dermatomal Blistering Rash & Ophthalmic Risk
red_flags: Rash involving the tip of the nose, forehead, or around the eye (herpes zoster ophthalmicus—sight-threatening emergency)
Widespread rash across multiple dermatomes in an immunocompromised patient
Severe headache, confusion, or facial weakness (Ramsay Hunt syndrome)
recommended_specialty_ar: الأمراض الجلدية والتناسلية / الباطنة العامة
content: Shingles is a reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus causing a painful, burning, or tingling sensation on one side of the body, followed days later by a red rash that develops into fluid-filled blisters along a single nerve band (dermatome) without crossing the midline. Early antiviral medication within 72 hours of rash onset shortens illness and reduces postherpetic neuralgia risk.

title: Cellulitis – Spreading Skin Erythema & Sepsis Red Flags
red_flags: Rapidly spreading red, hot, swollen skin accompanied by high fever, shivering, rapid heartbeat, or confusion (sepsis)
Severe pain out of proportion to skin appearance, blisters, or skin necrosis (necrotizing fasciitis)
Redness and swelling around the eye (orbital or periorbital cellulitis)
recommended_specialty_ar: الأمراض الجلدية / الباطنة العامة والجراحة
content: Cellulitis is an acute bacterial skin infection that causes a poorly demarcated area of red, hot, swollen, and tender skin, most commonly on the lower leg, often entering through a cut, insect bite, or cracked skin. Prompt oral antibiotics treat mild localized cellulitis, while systemic fever or rapid spread requires urgent hospital intravenous antibiotics.

title: Iron Deficiency Anemia – Pallor, Fatigue & Occult Bleeding Triage
red_flags: Anemia symptoms accompanied by black tarry stools, vomiting blood, or rectal bleeding
Chest pain, shortness of breath at rest, or fainting due to severe anemia
Unexplained iron-deficiency anemia in men or postmenopausal women (requires GI malignancy screening)
recommended_specialty_ar: أمراض الدم / الباطنة العامة والجهاز الهضمي
content: Iron deficiency anemia occurs when low iron levels reduce hemoglobin production, impairing oxygen transport. Symptoms include persistent tiredness, lack of energy, shortness of breath on exertion, noticeable heart palpitations, pale skin, headaches, and brittle nails. Evaluation involves a complete blood count (CBC), serum ferritin, iron supplementation, and identifying underlying blood loss or malabsorption.

title: Hypothyroidism (Underactive Thyroid) – Fatigue, Cold Intolerance & Weight Gain
red_flags: Severe drowsiness, hypothermia, slow heart rate, and confusion (myxedema coma—medical emergency)
Rapidly enlarging thyroid neck mass with hoarseness or difficulty swallowing
recommended_specialty_ar: الغدد الصماء والسكري / الباطنة العامة
content: An underactive thyroid gland (hypothyroidism) does not produce enough thyroid hormones, slowing down the body's metabolism. Common symptoms include chronic tiredness, sensitivity to cold, unexplained weight gain, constipation, depression, dry skin, brittle hair, and muscle aches. Diagnosis is confirmed with TSH and free T4 blood tests and treated with daily levothyroxine.

title: Diabetes Mellitus – Hyperglycemia Symptoms & DKA Emergency Red Flags
red_flags: Excessive thirst and urination accompanied by nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, deep rapid breathing, fruity breath, or confusion (diabetic ketoacidosis / DKA)
Severe hypoglycemia with sweating, trembling, confusion, seizures, or loss of consciousness
Infected diabetic foot ulcer with spreading redness or fever
recommended_specialty_ar: الغدد الصماء والسكري / الباطنة العامة
content: Diabetes is a chronic metabolic disease characterized by elevated blood glucose levels. Classic symptoms of hyperglycemia include excessive thirst (polydipsia), frequent urination (polyuria), unexplained weight loss, blurred vision, slow-healing wounds, and persistent fatigue. Vomiting, abdominal pain, and drowsiness with high blood sugar indicate life-threatening diabetic ketoacidosis requiring immediate emergency hospital treatment.

title: Atopic Dermatitis (Eczema) – Pruritic Flexural Rash & Secondary Infection
red_flags: Widespread painful punched-out blisters on eczematous skin with fever (eczema herpeticum—urgent dermatology/antiviral care)
Yellow crusting, pus, spreading warmth, and fever indicating secondary bacterial skin infection
recommended_specialty_ar: الأمراض الجلدية والحساسية
content: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is a chronic inflammatory skin condition causing dry, intensely itchy, inflamed skin patches, commonly in the inner elbows, behind the knees, hands, neck, and face. Scratching worsens inflammation and causes thickened, cracked, or weeping skin. Management relies on frequent emollient moisturizers, avoiding triggers, and short courses of topical corticosteroids.
